1 --- 2 title: Designing view transitions 3 description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app. 4 nav_title: View transitions 5 --- 6 7 In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that. 8 9 Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states. 10 11 React's `` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions. 12 13 This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route. 14 15 ## Use the vercel-react-view-transitions skill 16 17 The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/tree/main/skills/react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app. 18 19 Install the skill: 20 21 ```bash filename="Terminal" 22 npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill vercel-react-view-transitions 23 ``` 24 25 Then give the agent this prompt: 26 27 ```prompt 28 Add view transitions to this app using the vercel-react-view-transitions skill. 29 ``` 30 31 To apply the patterns yourself, follow the walkthrough below. 32 33 ## Example 34 35 As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_. 36 37 We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions). 38 39 You can find the resources used in this example here: 40 41 - [Demo](https://react-view-transitions-demo.labs.vercel.dev) 42 - [Code](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo) 43 44 View transitions work in the App Router with no configuration. The App Router uses [React canary releases](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries), which contain all stable React 19 changes as well as newer features like `ViewTransition`. You do not need to install `react@canary` yourself. 45 46 > [!NOTE] 47 > React's integration uses newer View Transitions API features (transition types and `view-transition-class`), available in Chromium 125+ and recent Safari and Firefox versions. Some animations may behave differently in Safari. Without browser support, your application works normally; the transitions do not animate. 48 49 Import the `ViewTransition` component from React: 50 51 ```tsx 52 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 53 ``` 54 55 `` animations are activated by [Transitions](https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition), [``](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense), and [`useDeferredValue`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useDeferredValue). Regular `setState` calls do not trigger them. In Next.js, route navigations are transitions, so `` animations activate automatically during navigation. 56 57 ### Step 1: Morph a thumbnail into a hero image 58 59 The gallery displays photos in a grid. Clicking a photo opens a detail page with a larger version of the same image. Without transitions, the thumbnail disappears and the hero appears. Nothing connects them visually. The user has to scan the detail page to confirm they clicked the right photo. 60 61 In motion design, when an object persists across a cut, it communicates continuity. The viewer understands they are looking at the same thing, not a replacement. This is the most important transition pattern: **shared element morphing**. 62 63 Wrap both the grid thumbnail and the detail hero in `` with the same `name`: 64 65 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 66 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 67 import Image from 'next/image' 68 import Link from 'next/link' 69 70 function PhotoGrid({ photos }) { 71 return ( 72
73 {photos.map((photo) => ( 74 75 76 77 78 79 ))} 80
81 ) 82 } 83 ``` 84 85 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/photo-content.tsx" 86 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 87 import Image from 'next/image' 88 89 async function PhotoContent({ id }) { 90 const photo = await getPhoto(id) 91 92 return ( 93 94
95 96
97 98 ) 99 } 100 ``` 101 102 The `name` prop creates identity. React finds elements with the same name on the old and new pages, then animates between their size and position automatically. No additional props are needed for the morph to work. 103 104 If we click a thumbnail now, the image scales and repositions from its grid cell to the hero slot. Navigating back reverses the morph. The user sees one object moving, not two objects swapping. 105 106 The morph plays when the destination content renders in the same commit as the navigation, which is the case with prefetched (cached) pages. If the destination suspends into a fallback first, no pair forms, and the content animates with its enter animation instead when it arrives. 107 108 #### Customizing the morph animation 109 110 The morph works without any CSS. To customize it, add `share="morph"` together with `default="none"`. The `share` prop assigns the `morph` class to the view transition, which you can target with CSS pseudo-elements. **Theme setup**
- Imports Tailwind, `tw-animate-css`, and a shadcn stylesheet, then uses `@theme inline` to bridge CSS variables into Tailwind tokens (colors, fonts, sidebar tokens, chart colors).

**Keyframes** (four total)
- `fade` — animates from `filter: blur(3px); opacity: 0;` to unblurred and fully opaque.
- `slide` — translates from `var(--slide-offset)` to `0`.
- `slide-y` — vertical translate using `var(--slide-y-offset, 10px)`.
- `via-blur` — a mid-animation blur spike at the 30% mark.

**View transition rules**
- `fade-out` / `fade-in`: old view plays `fade` reversed; new view plays it forward after the exit delay.
- `slide-down` / `slide-up`: combine fade and `slide-y`, reversed on exit.
- `nav-forward` / `nav-back`: mirrored pairs setting `--slide-offset` to ±60px so content slides in the direction of navigation, combined with fade.
- `morph`: group duration set to the move variable; the image pair uses `via-blur`.

**Pointer events**
- `::view-transition { pointer-events: none; }` — the comment explains the overlay would otherwise swallow all pointer input, and notes that named participants are still skipped during hit-testing as "spec behavior with no CSS override."

Five named groups — site header, gallery controls, back link, prev and next nav — get `animation: none` and `z-index: 100`; their `-old` pseudo-elements are hidden with `display: none` and their `-new` ones are also unanimated, so they appear static across transitions.

**Base layer**
Applies border and outline utilities to `*`, background/foreground to `body`, sans font to `html`, and styles WebKit scrollbars at 6px with a translucent white thumb (`border-radius: 3px`) that brightens on hover.

content.text:
Done. All four transition patterns are in place.

## What I found first

The installed Next.js (`16.3.1-canary.3`) ships an agent-facing warning that its APIs differ from training data, plus a bundled guide at `node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/02-guides/view-transitions.md` covering this exact task. I followed that over my priors, which mattered — two of my initial assumptions were wrong:

- **No config flag and no `unstable_` prefix.** It's `import { ViewTransition } from 'react'`, working in the App Router with zero config. Root `react` is pinned to 19.1.0 (no `ViewTransition`), but Next aliases the App Router to its vendored `19.3.0-canary`, which has it. I verified the alias resolves at runtime rather than trusting the doc.
- **No type shim needed.** I initially added a `/// <reference types="react/canary" />` file, then checked whether it was load-bearing — `next/dist/types.d.ts` already pulls in `react/experimental` → `react/canary` transitively, so I deleted it. My first test of this was a false pass from the incremental `tsc` cache; I re-ran with the cache cleared to confirm.

## Changes

- **`app/transitions.ts`** (new) — shared `navDirection` type→class map and the `productImageName` helper, so the morph names on the two pages can't drift apart.
- **`app/ProductGrid.tsx`** — thumbnail wrapped in `<ViewTransition name={...} share="morph" default="none">`; `Link` tagged `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`.
- **`app/product/[slug]/page.tsx`** — hero wrapped with the matching name; back link tagged `nav-back`; Suspense fallback/content wrapped in `slide-down`/`slide-up`.
- **`app/page.tsx`** — same Suspense reveal on the grid, plus the directional page wrapper.
- **`app/globals.css`** — morph (400ms with a mid-flight blur to hide interpolation artifacts), asymmetric Suspense reveal (150ms exit, 210ms enter delayed behind it), ±60px directional slides, `::view-transition { pointer-events: none }` so clicks mid-animation aren't swallowed, and the reduced-motion block.

Two deliberate choices worth flagging. The hero stays **outside** the Suspense boundary — if the destination suspends into a fallback first, no shared-element pair forms and the morph silently degrades to a plain enter. And the directional wrappers are in each `page.tsx`, not the layout, since layouts persist and `enter`/`exit` never fire there.

For reduced motion I used the documented approach: zero out all `::view-transition-*` durations and delays so content swaps instantly. I also gated the pre-existing `pulse` skeleton animation, which was an infinite animation ignoring the preference. The guide notes a more refined option that keeps opacity crossfades while dropping only positional movement — worth doing if you want reduced-motion users to still get a soft fade, but it's more CSS surface than I'd add without being able to eyeball it.

## Verification

`next build` compiles and typechecks clean; all 3 routes generate. Against a running production server I confirmed React emits its markers (`vt-name` / `vt-share="morph"` / `vt-enter` / `vt-exit`) and that `vt-name="product-image-classic-sneakers"` is byte-identical on the grid and detail page — so the morph pair actually forms. The `nav-forward`/`nav-back` maps travel in the RSC payload rather than the static chunks (they're server→client props), which I checked there.

One gap: no browser is available in this sandbox, so I could not watch the animations run. Everything up to the browser boundary is verified, but the visual timing and easing are unconfirmed — worth a look in Chromium.

Unrelated pre-existing issue I noticed and did not touch: the detail page's root is a bare `<div>`, so it misses the `max-width`/`padding` that `globals.css` applies to `main`, leaving that page flush to the viewport edge. Independent of transitions, but you may want it consistent since the slide now moves both pages side by side.
